table.title: Effects of perturbation magnitude during continuous action on physiological responses (2023AS04)
table.research_questions:
Theoretical hypothesis: Stress resulting from task-related perturbations in continuous action modulates physiological responses.

In the present study, we will prepare three conditions: the No-perturbation condition (Baseline condition), the Weak perturbation condition (Weak condition), and the Strong perturbation condition (Strong condition). In the Baseline condition, there are no perturbations during control. In the Weak condition, the degree of perturbation changes between 6 degrees and 15 degrees periodically. In the Strong condition, the degree of perturbation changes between 45 degrees and 75 degrees periodically.

Main working hypothesis: 
For the 1st Dependent variable: Skin Conductance Level (SCL)
H0: There is no significant difference in SCL among the weak, strong, and baseline conditions.
H1: There is a significant difference in SCL among the weak, strong, and baseline conditions.
If H1 is supported, the following pairwise hypotheses will be tested:
-H1-1: SCL is significantly higher in the weak condition than in the baseline condition. 
-H1-2: SCL is significantly higher in the strong condition than in the baseline condition. 
If either H1-1 or H1-2 is supported, the following hypothesis will be tested.
-H1-3: SCL is significantly higher in the strong condition than in the weak condition. 

For the 2nd Dependent variable: Sense of Agency (SoA) rating
H0: There is no difference, or SoA ratings are equal to or higher in the strong condition compared to the weak condition.
H1: SoA ratings are significantly lower in the strong condition than in the weak condition.

For the 3rd Dependent variable: Stress rating
H0: There is no difference, or Stress ratings are equal to or lower in the strong condition compared to the weak condition.
H1: Stress ratings are significantly higher in the strong condition than in the weak condition.

Note: Both SoA and stress ratings are collected at the end of each trial. Therefore, each rating reflects the participant’s experience during the entire trial, which includes both the baseline and either the weak or strong condition.

For the 4th Dependent variable: The number of successful reaches
H0: There is no difference, or the number of successful reaches is equal to or larger in the strong condition compared to the weak condition.
H1: The number of successful reaches is significantly smaller in the strong condition than in the weak condition.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
When the task starts, a gray game window (19.8 cm x 19.8 cm) will be displayed in the center of the black screen of a 23.8-inch LCD monitor with a resolution of 1920×1080 pixels.　Participants are seated approximately 60 cm away from the monitor. The experiment consists of one practice trial followed by two test trials. After the practice trial, physiological recording equipment is attached to the participant’s non-dominant hand. Electrodermal activity (EDA) electrodes (EL507 and LEAD110A  with EDA100C amplifier) are placed on the index and ring fingers, and a photoplethysmography (PPG) sensor (TSD200 with PPG100C amplifier) is placed on the middle finger. All signals are recorded at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz using Biopac Systems, Inc. (USA). A low-pass filter with a cutoff frequency of 1.0 Hz is applied. A brief recording check is then performed to ensure proper signal acquisition. Participants are instructed to keep their non-dominant hand, on which the physiological recording systems are attached, at rest without any movement.
Each trial begins with a 120-second resting period, during which participants are instructed to remain seated and refrain from any activity. Immediately after the resting period, five visual stimuli are presented on the screen: a red circular cursor (1.1 cm in diameter), three blue square distractors, and a yellow square target (each square measuring 1.1 cm per side). Each of the four squares is randomly positioned within a different quadrant area and remains fixed in that position throughout the experiment.
During each trial, participants control the red circular cursor using a joystick (Ultra Joystick, Pretorian Technologies Ltd.) with their dominant hand and are required to reach the yellow target while avoiding the blue obstacle. Upon successfully reaching the target, one of the three blue obstacles changes to yellow and becomes the next target, while the original yellow target turns into a blue obstacle. Participants continue to control the cursor and reach targets until the trial ends.
There are two experimental conditions: Weak and Strong perturbation conditions. In general, perturbation refers to rotating the cursor’s displayed position clockwise relative to its actual position. With regard to the perturbation, participants are informed that “A computer-controlled interference may sometimes occur, resulting in a disturbance of cursor movement.” In the Weak perturbation condition, the degree of perturbation changes between 6 degrees and 15 degrees periodically; in each cycle, the cursor deviates by 15 degrees within 5 seconds after perturbation onset, then gradually shifts to 6 degrees over the following 3 seconds, and returns to 15 degrees over an additional 3 seconds. In the Strong perturbation condition, the degree of perturbation changes between 45 degrees and 75 degrees periodically; in each cycle, the cursor deviates by 75 degrees within 5 seconds after perturbation onset, then gradually shifts to 45 degrees over the following 3 seconds, and returns to 75 degrees over an additional 3 seconds.
The practice trial consists of a 20-second resting period and a 60-second joystick control period without any perturbation (i.e., baseline period). Each test trial consists of a 120-second resting period, a 360-second baseline period, a 143-second perturbation period (either Weak or Strong condition), and a 90-second post-perturbation baseline period.
At the end of each trial, participants are asked to rate their subjective Sense of Agency (SoA) and perceived stress. For SoA, they answer the question, “How much control did you feel over the movement of the red circle？”, using a 9-point Likert scale (1 = No control, 9 = Full control). For subjective stress, they respond to the question, “How stressed were you about controlling the red circle on screen？”, also using a 9-point Likert scale (1 = Not at all, 9 = Very much). Responses are submitted by clicking on the appropriate option on the Likert scales using a mouse.
A rest period of approximately three minutes is provided after each trial, during which the physiological recording equipment remains attached to the participant. The procedure for the second test trial is identical to that of the first, except for the magnitude of the perturbation.
The experiment employs a fully within-participant design with one factor: perturbation condition (Weak vs. Strong). Each participant completes one practice trial and two test trials. Each test trial lasts approximately 10 minutes, and the entire experiment is completed in approximately 60 minutes.
table.randomization: The order of conditions is counterbalanced across participants.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to any human observation of the data
table.data_collection_procedures: Undergraduates, graduates, and research students at Kyushu University in Japan will participate in this experiment for approximately 60 minutes. They will be recruited via SNS (an official LINE account of our laboratory).
table.sample_size: We primarily focus on whether SCL in the Strong condition is significantly larger than in the Weak condition (i.e., H1-3). Therefore, we conducted a power analysis for a one-tailed paired sample t-test using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007), which suggested that a sample of 45 participants would be needed to detect an effect size (d) of 0.5 with power of 0.95 (1-β err prob) and α err prob of 0.05. Based on this, our target sample size is determined to be at least 45 participants.  Considering the possibility of exclusion of participants, we plan to recruit 48 participants for this experiment.
table.sample_size_rationale:
The minimum sample size was calculated based on:
Faul, F., Erdfelder, E., Lang, A. G., & Buchner, A. (2007). G* Power 3: A flexible statistical power analysis program for the social, behavioral, and biomedical sciences. Behavior research methods, 39(2), 175-191.
table.manipulated_variables: We will manipulate one within-participant factor: the perturbation between the participant’s control and cursor movement. This factor has two levels: Weak perturbation and Strong perturbation.
table.measured_variables: We will record electrodermal activity (EDA) and photoplethysmography (PPG) throughout the experiment. PPG measurement will be conducted solely to verify that the device is functioning properly and will not be included in the analysis. Additionally, we will count the number of successful reaches for each experimental condition. At the end of each experimental trial, participants will also provide subjective ratings of their SoA over the cursor's movement on a 9-point Likert scale (1 = No control, 9 = Full control), and their perceived subjective stress related to cursor control on a 9-point Likert scale (1 = Not at all, 9 = Very much).
table.indices: For each experimental trial, based on the digital trigger (PLDM-20, Sankei Kizai Co., Ltd., onset of a white stimulus in the down-left corner in the screen) in the raw EDA data, we will compute the median EDA value during the 60 seconds preceding the perturbation as the baseline EDA for the current trial, and the mean EDA value during the 60 seconds following the perturbation onset as the SCL data for the current trial in each condition. These values will be used in subsequent data analyses.
table.statistical_tests:
Manipulation check
As manipulation checks, we will first conduct one-tailed paired t-tests to examine whether (1) the subjective SoA rating in the Weak condition is significantly higher than that in the Strong condition, and (2) the subjective stress rating in the Weak condition is significantly lower than that in the Strong condition.  
To test whether perturbation strength significantly affects performance (the number of successful reaches during the cursor movement perturbation), we will fit a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a Poisson distribution and a log link function (formula: SuccessCount ~ Perturbation  + (1 | ParticipantID)  . In this model, SuccessCount is a count data representing the number of successful reaches, and Perturbation is a categorical fixed effect indicating the perturbation strength (Weak and Strong), and (1 | ParticipantID) denotes a random intercept to account for repeated measures within participants.

Experimental analysis
We will conduct one-tailed paired sample t-tests to analyze the data.
We will examine whether the SCL during the perturbation period is significantly higher than that during the baseline period for the Weak condition. The planned analyses are as follows:
Analysis 1: Test whether the SCL during the perturbation period in the Weak condition is significantly higher than the SCL during the Baseline condition.
Analysis 2: Test whether the SCL during the perturbation period in the Strong condition is significantly higher than the SCL during the Baseline condition.
Analysis 3 will be conducted if Analysis 1 and Analysis 2 (or Analysis 2 alone) show significant differences.
In Analysis 3, we will test whether the increase in SCL from baseline during the perturbation period is significantly greater in the Strong condition than in the Weak condition (i.e., SCL_Strong − SCL_Baseline vs. SCL_Weak − SCL_Baseline).
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p < .05 criteria to determine if the t-test suggests that the results significantly differ from those expected if the null hypothesis were correct.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Participants whose EDA data cannot be properly recorded will be excluded from the data analysis. Specifically, participants whose average EDA during the continuous target-reaching task is below 2 μS will be excluded.
table.missing_data_handling: We will not deal with missing data.
table.exploratory_analyses: We plan to divide the 60 seconds following the onset of the perturbation into 12 evenly spaced 5-second segments (or into six evenly spaced 10-second segments). For each segment, we will calculate the average SCL and subtract it from the SCL measured during the Baseline condition to obtain the baseline-corrected SCL. To examine whether the difference in SCL between the Weak and Strong perturbation conditions varies over time, we will fit a linear mixed-effects model (LMM) with baseline-corrected SCL as the dependent variable. The model will include Perturbation Strength (treated as a categorical variable; Weak and Strong), Time Segment (treated as a categorical variable or ordinal variable), and their interaction as fixed effects, as well as a random intercept for each participant to account for within-subject variability. We will also examine whether using 90- or 120-second segments after the onset of the perturbation produces similar results to using the 60-second segment.

table.title: Effects of perturbation duration during continuous action on physiological responses (2023AS05)
table.research_questions:
Theoretical hypothesis: Task-related perturbations during continuous action induce stress associated with reduced controllability, thereby modulating physiological responses.

The present study will include two perturbation conditions: a Short-term perturbation condition and a Long-term perturbation condition. In the Short-term perturbation condition, the perturbation angle cyclically alternates between 30° and 75° for 31s. In the Long-term perturbation condition, the perturbation angle cyclically alternates between 30° and 75° for 143 s. In addition, each experimental trial includes a no-perturbation baseline period, which is treated as the Baseline condition. During this period, participants perform the control task without any external perturbation.

Main working hypothesis: 
For the 1st Dependent variable: Electrodermal Activity (EDA)
H0: There is no significant difference in EDA among the Short-term, Long-term, and Baseline conditions.

table.study_design_overview:
When the task starts, a gray game window measuring 19.8 cm × 19.8 cm is displayed at the center of a black screen on a 23.8-inch LCD monitor with a resolution of 1920 × 1080 pixels. Participants are seated approximately 60 cm away from the monitor.
The present experiment employs a fully within-participant design with one factor, perturbation duration, consisting of two conditions: Short-term perturbation and Long-term perturbation. Each participant completes one practice trial followed by two experimental trials, one for each perturbation-duration condition.
After the practice trial, physiological recording equipment is attached to the participant’s non-dominant hand and remains in place throughout the experimental session. EDA is recorded using electrodes placed on the index and ring fingers of the non-dominant hand. The electrodes are connected to an EDA100C amplifier using EL507 electrodes and LEAD110A leads. Photoplethysmography (PPG) is recorded using a TSD200 sensor connected to a PPG100C amplifier, with the sensor placed on the middle finger of the non-dominant hand. All signals are recorded at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz using Biopac Systems, Inc. (USA). A low-pass filter with a cutoff frequency of 1.0 Hz is applied to the EDA signal. A brief recording check is then performed to ensure proper signal acquisition. Participants are instructed to keep their non-dominant hand, to which the physiological recording equipment is attached, at rest and to avoid moving it throughout the task.
Each trial consists of a resting period followed by a joystick-control period. At the beginning of each trial, a countdown timer is displayed on the screen, and participants are instructed to remain seated and refrain from moving during the resting period. Immediately after the resting period, the task interface appears. The interface consists of five visual stimuli: one red circular cursor, three blue square distractors, and one yellow square target. Participants control the red cursor using a joystick operated with their dominant hand. Their task is to move the cursor toward the yellow target while avoiding contact with the blue distractors. Once the cursor reaches the target, one of the three distractors is randomly selected, changes color from blue to yellow and becomes the new target. At the same time, the previous target changes back to a blue distractor. Participants continue performing this target-reaching task until the end of the trial.
The practice trial consists of a 20 s resting period followed by a 60 s joystick-control period without any perturbation. Each experimental trial consists of a 120 s resting period followed by a 593 s joystick-control period. The joystick-control period is further divided into three periods: a baseline period, a perturbation period, and a post-perturbation baseline period. In the Short-term perturbation condition, the joystick-control period includes a 360 s baseline period, a 31 s perturbation period, and a 202 s post-perturbation baseline period. In the Long-term perturbation condition, the joystick-control period includes a 360 s baseline joystick-control period, a 143 s perturbation period, and a 90 s post-perturbation baseline period. Thus, the total duration of the joystick-control period is identical across the two experimental conditions. 
Perturbation refers to a clockwise rotation of the visual feedback of cursor movement relative to the participant’s joystick input. Participants are informed that “a computer-controlled interference may sometimes occur, resulting in a disturbance of cursor movement.”
At the onset of the perturbation period, the perturbation angle gradually increases from 0° to 75° over 5 s and then remains at 75° for 5 s, constituting the ramp-up phase of the perturbation period. Subsequently, the perturbation angle cyclically alternates between 75° and 30°, constituting the cycle phase of the perturbation period. Within each cycle, the perturbation angle first gradually decreases from 75° to 30° over 3 s, remains at 30° for 5 s, gradually increases back to 75° over 3 s, and then remains at 75° for another 5 s. Thus, each complete cycle lasts 16 s. In the Short-term condition, the cycle phase consists of a single full cycle, lasting 16 s. In the Long-term condition, the cycle phase consists of eight full cycles, lasting 128 s in total. Following the cycle phase, the perturbation angle gradually decreases from 75° to 0° over 5 s, constituting the recovery phase of the perturbation period. Thereafter, no perturbation is applied, and the trial continues under a post-perturbation baseline until the end.
A rest interval of approximately 3 min is provided between two experimental trials, during which the physiological recording equipment remained attached to the participant. The entire experiment lasts approximately 60 min, with each experimental trial lasting approximately 12 min in total.
At the end of each trial, participants complete subjective ratings of SoA and perceived stress. SoA is assessed using the question, “How much control did you feel over the movement of the red circle?” Responses are provided on a 9-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (No control) to 9 (Full control). Perceived stress is assessed using the question, “How stressed were you about controlling the red circle on screen?” Responses are also recorded on a 9-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Not at all) to 9 (Very much). Participants submit their responses by selecting the corresponding option on the screen using a mouse.
table.randomization: The order of the two experimental conditions is counterbalanced across participants.
table.data_collection_procedures: Undergraduates, graduates, and research students at Kyushu University in Japan will participate in this experiment.
table.sample_size: Our primary interest is whether baseline-corrected EDA during the critical 60-s analysis window in the Long-term condition is significantly higher than EDA in the Short-term condition (i.e., H1-3). Therefore, we conducted a priori power analysis for a one-tailed paired sample t-test using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007), which suggested that a sample of 45 participants would be needed to detect an effect size (d) of 0.5 with power of 0.95 (1-β err prob) and α err prob of 0.05. Based on this, our target sample size is determined to be at least 45 participants. Considering the possibility of exclusion of participants, we plan to recruit 48 participants for this experiment.
table.manipulated_variables: We will manipulate one within-participant factor: the perturbation duration within a single trial. This factor has two levels: Short-term perturbation condition and Long-term perturbation condition.
table.measured_variables: We will record EDA and photoplethysmography (PPG) throughout the experiment. PPG measurement will be conducted solely to verify that the device is functioning properly and will not be included in the analysis. Additionally, we will count the number of successful reaches for each experimental condition. At the end of each experimental trial, participants will also provide subjective ratings of their SoA over the cursor's movement on a 9-point Likert scale (1 = No control, 9 = Full control), and their perceived subjective stress related to cursor control on a 9-point Likert scale (1 = Not at all, 9 = Very much).
table.indices:
For each experimental trial, perturbation onset will be identified based on the digital trigger recorded in the raw EDA data. The trigger is generated by a PLDM-20 device (Sankei Kizai Co., Ltd.) and corresponds to the onset of a white stimulus presented in the lower-left corner of the screen.
For each trial, we will compute the median EDA value during the 60 s immediately preceding perturbation onset as the baseline EDA for that trial. We will then compute the mean EDA value during the critical 60-s analysis window, defined as the period from 31 s to 91 s after perturbation onset. 
For each condition, Baseline-corrected EDA will be calculated by subtracting baseline EDA from mean EDA during the critical 60-s analysis window as follows:
EDA increase in the Short-term condition = mean EDA during the 31–91 s window after perturbation onset in the Short-term condition − baseline EDA in the same trial
EDA increase in the Long-term condition = mean EDA during the 31–91 s window after perturbation onset in the Long-term condition − baseline EDA in the same trial
Note that, in the Short-term perturbation condition, the perturbation ends 31 s after perturbation onset. Therefore, this critical analysis window corresponds to the 60-s period immediately after perturbation offset. In the Long-term perturbation condition, the perturbation continues for 143 s. Therefore, the same critical analysis window remains within the perturbation period.
table.statistical_tests:
For the EDA data, we will first conduct one-tailed paired-samples t-tests to analyze whether EDA during the critical analysis window in the Short-term perturbation condition is significantly higher than baseline EDA in the same trial. Next, we will test whether EDA during the critical analysis window in the Long-term perturbation condition is significantly higher than baseline EDA in the same trial. Furthermore, we will test whether the baseline-corrected EDA differs significantly between the Short-term and Long-term perturbation conditions. 

To examine the temporal dynamics of baseline-corrected EDA and whether this temporal pattern differs between the Short-term and Long-term perturbation conditions, we will conduct a generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) analysis. For this analysis, the dependent variable will be baseline-corrected EDA during the critical 60-s analysis window. The model will include perturbation condition (Short-term vs. Long-term) as a fixed effect, condition-specific smooth functions of time, and participant-specific smooth functions of time. Time will be represented by time bins within the critical 60-s analysis window. The condition-specific smooth functions will allow the temporal trajectory of baseline-corrected EDA to vary nonlinearly between the Short-term and Long-term perturbation conditions. The participant-specific smooth functions will account for individual differences in EDA response trajectories over time.
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p < .05 criteria to determine if the t-test suggests that the results significantly differ from those expected if the null hypothesis were correct.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Participants whose EDA data cannot be properly recorded will be excluded from the data analysis. Specifically, participants whose EDA mean during the continuous target-reaching task is below 2 μS will be excluded. In addition, participants whose data collection is incomplete due to unforeseen circumstances during the experiment will also be excluded.

text.text: Sense of agency (SoA) refers to the subjective feeling of controlling one's own actions and their outcomes.

Previous studies have shown that sensorimotor discrepancies, such as spatial perturbations, reduce SoA, but it remains unclear whether such control disruptions also elicit online autonomic arousal during continuous action.
In the present study, across two experiments, participants performed a continuous target-reaching task in which visual feedback of cursor movement was spatially perturbed.
We recorded electrodermal activity during the task and used skin conductance level (SCL) as the physiological measure.
We assessed subjective SoA and perceived stress after each trial.
In Experiment 1, we manipulated perturbation magnitude and found that stronger perturbation reduced subjective SoA, increased perceived stress, and elicited a greater increase in SCL.

In Experiment 2, we manipulated perturbation duration to examine whether the SCL increase in Experiment 1 depended on the continued presence of a strong perturbation or primarily on the early phase of disrupted control.

Participants reported lower subjective SoA and higher perceived stress in the Long-term perturbation condition than in the Short-term perturbation condition, whereas mean SCL change did not reliably differ between conditions.
Together, these findings suggest that spatial perturbations during continuous action are accompanied by changes in sympathetic electrodermal activity.
The SCL was sensitive to perturbation magnitude, whereas evidence for a duration-related difference in mean SCL was limited.

Therefore, it remains unclear whether sensorimotor perturbations commonly used to modulate SoA also elicit increases in sympathetically mediated EDA.
In the present study, we examined whether control-related spatial perturbations during continuous action induce online physiological changes in EDA.
Specifically, we focused on skin conductance level (SCL) as an index of sympathetic electrodermal arousal.
Participants performed a continuous target-reaching task while the visual feedback of cursor movement was spatially perturbed.
In two experiments, we measured subjective SoA, perceived stress, and SCL during task performance.
In Experiment 1, we examined whether the magnitude of the perturbation modulates both subjective responses and physiological arousal by comparing Weak and Strong spatial perturbation conditions.
We hypothesized that stronger perturbation would reduce subjective SoA and increase perceived stress.
Furthermore, we predicted that stronger perturbation would elicit a larger increase in SCL relative to baseline.
In Experiment 2, we further examined whether the SCL increase following a strong perturbation depends on the continued presence of the perturbation or persists after the perturbation ends.
To this end, we compared Short-term and Long-term perturbation conditions.

Together, these experiments aimed to clarify whether spatial perturbations commonly used to manipulate SoA are accompanied by online autonomic arousal and whether such physiological changes are shaped by perturbation magnitude or duration.

Given the possibility of participant exclusion, we planned to recruit 48 participants for this experiment.
We recruited 48 participants (16 men, 32 women; 3 left-handed based on their selfreport; mean age = 22.13 years, SD = 3.42) from Kyushu University for the current experiment.
All participants were naïve to the purpose of the experiment, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and provided written informed consent.
Each participant received 1,000 JPY for the experiment (approximately 7 USD).

Experiments 1 and 2 were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and were approved by the local ethics committee of the Graduate School of Human-Environment Studies, Kyushu University (Approval Nos. 2026-008, 2025-005, and 2023-038).
All stimuli were presented on a 23.8-inch LCD monitor (EIZO Corporation, Hakusan, Japan) with a refresh rate of 60 Hz and resolution of 1,920 × 1,080 pixels.
The viewing distance from the display was approximately 60 cm without a chin rest.
The experiment was programmed using MATLAB (R2019a, The MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA) with the Psychtoolbox extension (Brainard, 1997; Pelli, 1997).

text.text: During the experiment, a joystick (Ultra Joystick, Pretorian Technologies) was used to control the cursor.
EDA was recorded using an EDA100C amplifier and EL507 electrodes, and photoplethysmography (PPG) was recorded using a PPG100C amplifier and a TSD200 transducer.
Signals were acquired at a sampling rate of 1,000 Hz using a Biopac MP160 data acquisition system and AcqKnowledge 5.0 software (BIOPAC Systems Inc., Goleta, CA, USA).
The EDA100C gain was set to 5 µS/V. Both high-pass filter settings (0.05 and 0.5 Hz) were set to DC, and the hardware low-pass filter was set to 1.0 Hz.

The physiological recording devices were attached to the participant's non-dominant hand: EDA electrodes were placed on the index and ring fingers, and a PPG optical sensor was attached to the middle finger.
Note that PPG was recorded to monitor device operation but was not included in the preregistered or main analyses.
We applied no additional software filtering to the EDA signal during acquisition.
In the experimental task, a gray game window (19.8 cm × 19.8 cm) was presented at the center of the monitor against a black background.

Five visual stimuli were presented within the game window: a red circular cursor (1.1 cm in diameter), three blue square distractors, and one yellow square target (each square measuring 1.1 cm × 1.1 cm).
The four squares were randomly positioned within four different quadrants of the game window and remained fixed in those positions throughout the trial.
The experiment consisted of one practice trial and two experimental trials.
Each trial consisted of a resting period followed by a continuous target-reaching task.
At the beginning of each trial, a countdown timer was displayed on the screen, and participants were instructed to remain seated and relaxed and refrain from movement during the resting period.
After the resting period, the task interface appeared, consisting of five visual stimuli: one red circular cursor, three blue square distractors, and one yellow square target.
Participants controlled the red cursor using a joystick operated with their dominant hand.
Their task was to move the cursor toward the yellow target while avoiding contact with the blue distractors.

Once the cursor reached the target, one of the three distractors was randomly selected to change color from blue to yellow and became the new target, whereas the previous target reverted to a blue distractor.
Participants continuously repeated this target-reaching task until the end of the trial.
The practice trial consisted of a 20-s resting period followed by a 60-s joystickcontrol period without perturbation.
After the practice trial, physiological recording equipment was attached to the participant's non-dominant hand and remained in place throughout the experimental session.
Before the first experimental trial began, the EDA and PPG signals were visually inspected to confirm that physiological signals were being recorded.
Each experimental trial consisted of a 120-s resting period followed by a 593-s joystick-control period (i.e., approximately 12 min in total).

The joystick-control period was further divided into a 360-s baseline period (i.e., no perturbation), a 143-s perturbation period, and a 90-s post-perturbation baseline period (i.e., no perturbation).
A rest interval of approximately 3 min was provided between two experimental trials, during which the physiological recording equipment remained attached to the participant.
The entire experiment lasted approximately 60 min.
Experiment 1 employed a fully within-participant design with one factor: perturbation magnitude (Weak vs.
Strong).
In each trial, participants experienced one of two levels of angular perturbation, applied to the visual feedback of cursor movement.
Perturbation was defined as a clockwise rotation of the visual feedback of cursor movement relative to the participant's joystick input.
Participants were informed that computer-controlled interference might occasionally occur, resulting in disruptions to cursor movement.
The order of perturbation conditions was counterbalanced across participants.

At the onset of the perturbation period (i.e., after the 360-s baseline period), the perturbation angle gradually increased from 0° to the condition-specific maximum angle (15° in the Weak condition and 75° in the Strong condition) over 5 s and then remained at that angle for 5 s, constituting the ramp-up phase of the perturbation period (Figure 1).

text.text: The perturbation then entered the cycle phase, during which the angle alternated between the maximum and minimum angles assigned to each condition.
Specifically, the angle alternated between 15° and 6° in the Weak perturbation condition and between 75° and 30° in the Strong perturbation condition.
This angle alternation in the present study was adopted to prevent participants from adapting to (learning) the specific rotated angle.

In each cycle, the angle gradually decreased from the maximum to the minimum over 3 s, remained at the minimum for 5 s, increased back to the maximum over 3 s, and then remained at the maximum for another 5 s.
Thus, each complete cycle lasted 16 s.
In both perturbation conditions, the cycle phase consisted of eight complete cycles, lasting 128 s in total.
Following the cycle phase, the perturbation angle gradually decreased from the maximum angle to 0° over 5 s, constituting the recovery phase of the perturbation period.
Thereafter, no perturbation was applied, and the trial continued during the 90 s postperturbation baseline period until its conclusion.
At the end of each trial, participants completed subjective ratings of SoA and perceived stress.
SoA was assessed using the question, "How much control did you feel over the movement of the red circle?"
Responses were provided on a 9-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (No control) to 9 (Full control).
Perceived stress was assessed using the question, "How stressed were you about controlling the red circle on screen?"
Responses were also recorded on a 9-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Not at all) to 9 (Very much).
Participants submitted their responses by selecting the corresponding option on the screen using a mouse.

Each trial began with a 2-min countdown timer, corresponding to the resting period.
After the resting period, participants completed a 593-s continuous control task consisting of a baseline period, a perturbation period, and a post-perturbation baseline period.
During the task, participants controlled a red cursor with a joystick and moved it toward a yellow target while avoiding blue distractors.
The perturbation was defined as a clockwise rotation of the visual feedback of cursor movement relative to the participant's joystick input.

The blue trace represents the Strong perturbation condition, in which the perturbation angle alternated between 75° and 30°, whereas the red trace represents the Weak perturbation condition, in which the perturbation angle alternated between 15° and 6°.
In both conditions, the perturbation period consisted of eight complete cycles.
After each trial, participants rated their SoA and perceived stress on 9-point scales.
For each experimental trial, the perturbation onset was identified from the digital trigger recorded in the raw EDA data.
The trigger was generated by a PLDM-20 device (Sankei Kizai Co., Ltd.) and corresponded to the onset of a white stimulus presented in the lower-left corner of the screen.
For each trial, baseline SCL was defined as the median SCL value over the 60 s immediately preceding the perturbation onset.
We used the median for the baseline period to obtain a robust estimate of the pre-perturbation SCL level that was less influenced by transient, nonspecific fluctuations during this control period.
In contrast, we used the mean for the post-onset window because we aimed to quantify overall SCL activity after perturbation onset, including perturbation-related changes within the analysis window.
SCL during the post-onset analysis window was calculated as the mean SCL during the 60 s immediately following perturbation onset (0-60 s).
This window was selected to match the baseline window duration and capture the initial physiological response to the perturbation.
We did not use the full perturbation period of 143 s because such a long window may include habituation or adaptation to the perturbation, which could obscure the initial change in SCL.
Baseline-corrected SCL was then calculated separately for each condition by subtracting the baseline value from the mean value during the post-onset analysis window.
In the present study, we used R (version 4.5.1) in Visual Studio Code (version 1.124.2), primarily with the tidyverse package (2.0.0).
Data cleaning and restructuring were performed by dplyr (1.1.4) and tidyr (1.3.1), and data visualization was performed using ggplot2 (3.5.2).
To supplement the frequentist analyses by quantifying the strength of evidence, we computed Bayes factors in JASP (Version 0.97.1) for all directional paired-samples comparisons.

One-sided Bayesian paired-samples t-tests with the default Cauchy prior (r = 0.707) were used for comparisons analyzed with paired-samples t-tests, whereas a one-sided Bayesian Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for the exploratory nonparametric robustness check.
We report BF10 to quantify the evidence for the alternative hypothesis relative to the null.
Manipulation checks were conducted to confirm that the perturbation manipulation affected participants' subjective experience as intended.

First, one-tailed paired t-tests were conducted to examine whether subjective SoA rating was higher in the Weak perturbation condition than in the Strong perturbation condition, and whether subjective stress rating was lower in the Weak perturbation condition than in the Strong perturbation condition.
In addition, participants' task performance was compared between the two conditions by examining the number of successful target reaches in each condition.
The main analysis focused on changes in SCL from baseline to the post-onset analysis window (i.e., baseline-corrected SCL).
Directional hypotheses were tested using one-tailed paired t-tests.
Following the preregistered testing sequence, we first examined whether SCL during the post-onset analysis window was higher than baseline SCL separately in the Weak and Strong conditions.
If either test showed a significant difference, we then tested whether baseline-corrected SCL was greater in the Strong condition than in the Weak condition.
Of the 48 participants recruited for Experiment 1, 10 were excluded from the analyses.
Four participants were excluded because the digital trigger marking perturbation onset was not successfully recorded.

We excluded five participants whose mean SCL during the continuous target-reaching task remained below 2 μS in either Trial 1 or Trial 2, using the lower bound of the typical SCL range (2-20 μS; Dawson et al., 2017) as a criterion.

The primary analysis examined whether SCL increased from baseline to the postonset analysis window.

In the Weak condition, SCL during the post-onset analysis window (M = 7.70 μS, SD = 4.39) was not significantly higher than baseline SCL (M = 7.70 μS, SD = 4.23), t(37) = 0.07, p = .471, Cohen's dz = 0.01, BF10 = 0.18, indicating that weak perturbation did not elicit a reliable increase in SCL.

text.text: To explore population-level time-dependent changes in baseline-corrected SCL and estimate peak timing for each perturbation condition, we used an exploratory generalized additive mixed-effects model (GAMM), implemented in the mgcv package (version 1.9-3).
The GAMM allowed nonlinear temporal changes in SCL to be modeled while accounting for participant-level variability.
The model included the perturbation condition as a parametric predictor, condition-specific smooths of time, and participant-specific smooths over time.
To account for residual serial autocorrelation among the 1-s observations, we incorporated a first-order autoregressive [AR(1)] error structure.
The AR(1) parameter was estimated from the lag-1 correlation of residuals obtained from the corresponding GAMM without an autoregressive error structure.
Adjacent residual pairs were pooled across independent participant-by-condition time series, excluding pairs that crossed series boundaries.
The resulting estimate was ρ = .965, and the first observation of each time series was specified as the start of a new AR process.
The estimated population-level trajectories during the 60-s post-onset analysis window are shown in Figure 3B.

The Strong condition showed a model-estimated maximum approximately 11.4 s after perturbation onset.
Because the time smooth in the Weak condition was not significant, its numerical maximum was not interpreted as a reliable temporal peak.
These exploratory results suggest that the Strong condition showed a reliable nonlinear temporal change in SCL, whereas no reliable time-dependent change was detected in the Weak condition.
In Experiment 1, we examined whether spatial perturbations during continuous action elicit not only changes in subjective experience, but also online physiological activity indexed by SCL.

Consistent with previous studies, the results of Experiment 1 showed that stronger spatial perturbation led to lower SoA ratings (Farrer et al., 2008; Penton et al., 2022) and higher perceived stress, broadly consistent with previous findings that disrupted or delayed control can increase frustration (Miller & Mandryk, 2016), confirming that the current manipulation successfully altered participants' subjective experience of control.

text.text: Importantly, the SCL results showed that the Strong perturbation condition elicited a reliable increase in SCL relative to baseline, whereas the Weak perturbation condition did not.
Moreover, the baseline-corrected SCL was significantly higher in the Strong condition than in the Weak condition.
These results demonstrate that, in the present continuous-control task, stronger spatial perturbation can be accompanied by increased electrodermal activity.
The exploratory time-series analysis further suggested that the SCL in response to the Strong perturbation was not constant across the perturbation period.
The GAMM analysis indicated a nonlinear temporal pattern in the Strong condition, with the population-level predicted peak occurring approximately 11.4 s after perturbation onset.

The relatively early peak, followed by a gradual decline in SCL despite the continued presence of the perturbation, may reflect habituation to the altered sensorimotor environment (Barry et al., 2023; Meir et al., 2024; Zimmer & Richter, 2023).

text.text: Importantly, this temporal pattern raises two possible explanations for the increased SCL observed in the Strong condition.
One possibility is that the continued presence of the strong perturbation contributes to maintaining increased SCL, although its influence gradually diminishes over time.

Alternatively, the initial encounter with a strong perturbation may induce physiological arousal that persists for some time even after the perturbation itself is removed, potentially reflecting a physiological response triggered by the initial exposure to the perturbation or continued vigilance for further perturbations.

To distinguish between these possibilities, in Experiment 2, we examined whether the SCL following the initial increase depends on the continued presence of a strong perturbation or persists after the perturbation is removed.
We therefore manipulated perturbation duration while keeping its magnitude constant, comparing a Short-term perturbation condition with a Long-term perturbation condition.
We primarily focused on whether baseline-corrected SCL in the Long-term perturbation condition was significantly higher than in the Short-term perturbation condition.

Note that the procedure and parameters in the Long-term condition were completely identical to those in the Strong condition in Experiment 1.
After the onset of the perturbation, the perturbation angle increased from 0° to 75° over 5 s and remained at 75° for 5 s (i.e., the ramp-up phase).
The perturbation then entered the cycle phase, during which the angle alternated between 75° and 30°.
Each cycle lasted 16 s.
The cycle phase consisted of one cycle in the Short-term condition and eight cycles in the Long-term condition.
Finally, the perturbation angle decreased from 75° to 0° over 5 s (i.e., the recovery phase), after which the trial continued without perturbation until the end of the trial.
The data exclusion criteria were the same as in Experiment 1.
For each trial, baseline SCL was calculated as the median SCL value during the 60 s immediately preceding the perturbation onset, as in Experiment 1.
SCL during the critical analysis window was calculated as the mean SCL from 31 s to 91 s after perturbation onset, which differed from Experiment 1.
Baseline-corrected SCL was then calculated by subtracting baseline SCL from mean SCL during the critical 60-s analysis window separately for each condition.

Note that, in the Short-term perturbation condition, the perturbation ended 31 s after perturbation onset, indicating that the critical analysis window corresponded to the 60-s period immediately after perturbation offset.
In the Long-term perturbation condition, the perturbation continued for 143 s.
Therefore, the same critical analysis window remained within the perturbation period.

However, these differences should be interpreted cautiously because the ratings were obtained after the entire trial.
Thus, they may reflect not only the duration of the perturbation but also the duration of the subsequent unperturbed control period, which was longer in the Short-term condition.
The SCL analysis focused on the critical 60-s analysis window from 31 to 91 s after perturbation onset.
First, one-tailed paired t-tests were conducted to examine whether SCL increased relative to baseline in each condition.

In particular, the critical analysis window in the Short-term condition was set after the perturbation offset, indicating that baseline-corrected SCL remained elevated during the 60-s period following perturbation offset.

Finally, because the critical 60-s analysis window from 31 to 91 s after perturbation onset in the Short-term condition corresponded to the period immediately after perturbation offset, the absence of difference between the two conditions may have reflected residual arousal after the perturbation.
To examine this possibility, we conducted an additional exploratory analysis using a later 30-s window from 91 to 121 s after perturbation onset.

This window corresponded to a later phase of the ongoing perturbation in the Long-term condition and to a delayed post-perturbation period in the Short-term condition, approximately 60 to 90 s after perturbation offset.

Similar to the result targeting the 31 to 91s window, the SCL change did not differ significantly between the Long-term condition (M = 0.52 μS, SD = 1.63) and the Short-term condition (M = 0.20 μS, SD = 0.80), t(42) = 1.29, p = .102, Cohen's dz = 0.20, BF10 = 0.64.
A Wilcoxon signedrank test likewise showed no significant difference between conditions, W = 518, p = .297, BF10 = 0.35.
These results indicate that baseline-corrected SCL did not reliably differ between the Long-term and Short-term conditions during the later 91-121-s window.
However, this between-condition comparison alone does not establish whether SCL in the Short-term condition remained elevated relative to baseline.
In Experiment 2, we examined whether SCL increase after the peak depends on the continued presence of a strong perturbation or primarily on the early experience of that perturbation.
The results showed that participants reported lower SoA and higher perceived stress in the Long-term condition than in the Short-term condition.
Because the conditions also differed in the duration of unperturbed control before the retrospective ratings, these differences cannot be attributed uniquely to perturbation duration.
In contrast, the SCL results did not show clear evidence that longer perturbation exposure produced a larger physiological response.

Baseline-corrected SCL was significantly greater than zero in both the Short-term and Long-term conditions, but it did not differ significantly between conditions during the primary critical analysis window.

Importantly, in the Short-term condition, the critical analysis window occurred immediately after the perturbation had ended, whereas in the Long-term condition, the same window occurred while the perturbation was still ongoing.
This pattern suggests that SCL may remain elevated for some time after participants experience a strong perturbation, even after the perturbation itself disappears.

Taken together, the findings suggest that exposure to a strong perturbation in the Short-term condition was sufficient to elicit an increase in SCL that persisted after perturbation offset, whereas continuing the perturbation did not produce a reliably greater mean SCL increase over the corresponding analysis windows.
The present study examined whether control-related spatial perturbations during continuous action influence not only subjective SoA, but also online autonomic arousal indexed by SCL.
In Experiment 1, we manipulated perturbation magnitude and found that stronger perturbation reduced subjective SoA, increased perceived stress, and elicited a greater increase in SCL.

In Experiment 2, we manipulated perturbation duration to examine whether the SCL increase depended on the continued presence of a strong perturbation or primarily on the early experience of disrupted control.

Participants reported lower subjective SoA and higher perceived stress in the Long-term than in the Short-term perturbation condition, whereas mean baseline-corrected SCL did not reliably differ between conditions.

Together, these findings suggest that spatial perturbations during continuous action are accompanied by autonomic arousal, with the physiological response being sensitive to perturbation magnitude, whereas evidence for a duration-related difference in mean SCL was limited.
In Experiment 1, we found that SCL increased reliably relative to baseline in the Strong perturbation condition but not in the Weak perturbation condition.
Previous studies have experimentally manipulated arousal through procedures independent of sensorimotor discrepancy (Christensen et al., 2019; Chu et al., 2023; Wen et al., 2015a).
text.formatted: Previous studies have experimentally manipulated arousal through procedures independent of sensorimotor discrepancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Christensen et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Chu et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Wen et al., 2015a)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, to our knowledge, the present study is among the first to characterize tonic electrodermal changes and their temporal dynamics during graded visuomotor perturbation in continuous action.

The present finding extends the conventional interpretation of spatial perturbations: such perturbations not only disrupt sensorimotor correspondence and reduce subjective SoA but can also elicit online changes in autonomic arousal while an action is ongoing.

In addition, the exploratory GAMM analyses suggested that this physiological response unfolded dynamically in the Strong perturbation condition: the population-level predicted SCL rose steeply following perturbation onset, peaked approximately 11.38 s later, and then gradually declined.

The rapid initial increase may reflect an autonomic response to a salient sensorimotor discrepancy, and the subsequent decline, despite the continued presence of the perturbation, may reflect a reduction in the novelty and salience of the discrepancy.
In Experiment 2, we further clarified the temporal characteristics of these SCL changes.

When participants experienced the same strong perturbation for either a short or long duration, retrospective subjective SoA and perceived stress differed between the two duration conditions: ratings indicated lower SoA and higher stress in the Long-term condition than the Short-term condition.
In contrast, although SCL increased relative to baseline in both conditions, the magnitude of the increase did not differ significantly between them.

Importantly, the critical analysis window in the Short-term condition occurred immediately after perturbation offset, whereas the same window in the Longterm condition occurred during ongoing perturbation; this pattern therefore suggests that the early experience of a strong perturbation may be sufficient to elicit an increase in SCL that persists for some time after the perturbation disappears.
The exploratory GAMM analysis yielded a nonlinear trajectory in the Long-term condition and an approximately linear decline following the perturbation offset in the Short-term condition.

Taken together, the findings of Experiment 2 raise the possibility that continued exposure to a strong perturbation, as in the Long-term condition, may influence the temporal profile of the physiological response without necessarily amplifying its mean magnitude, but this possibility requires further confirmation.

Theoretically, the differences between the Long-term and Short-term conditions in retrospective SoA and perceived stress, in the absence of a corresponding difference in SCL, suggest that subjective experience and autonomic arousal need not covary directly but may reflect different temporal aspects of disrupted control.
The persistence of SCL elevation after perturbation offset also raises the possibility that the physiological consequences of disrupted control extend beyond the perturbation itself.

As an implication, whether such residual arousal carries over to subsequent actions remains unknown, but this possibility may be relevant to post-error adjustments, in which errors or difficult control experiences influence subsequent behavior (e.g., Danielmeier & Ullsperger, 2011; Di Costa et al., 2018).

text.text: Future studies could directly test whether perturbation-induced arousal predicts subsequent performance adjustments or agency judgments.
The present findings may extend the two-step account of SoA by suggesting that the consequences of spatial perturbation are not confined to sensorimotor processing.
Although the perturbation was introduced to alter the correspondence between predicted and observed cursor movements, it was accompanied by both reduced subjective SoA and increased SCL.
Thus, a sensorimotor manipulation commonly used to investigate SoA may also alter the agent's autonomic state.

Within the two-step account, bodily signals associated with this autonomic arousal could, in principle, provide an additional source of information for retrospective agency judgment (Herman & Tsakiris, 2020; Stern et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Within the two-step account, bodily signals associated with this autonomic arousal could, in principle, provide an additional source of information for retrospective agency judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Herman & Tsakiris, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Stern et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, even SoA judgments made in a relatively simple motor-control task may reflect the integration of sensorimotor prediction errors with bodily information arising from the disruption of control.

Moreover, the larger SCL change in the Strong condition raises the possibility that bodily information was more salient under severe control disruption and could have contributed to retrospective SoA judgment.
However, this possible contribution of bodily information does not imply a one-to-one correspondence between subjective judgments and SCL.
Rather, subjective ratings and physiological arousal may be sensitive to partially different temporal aspects of disrupted control.

Retrospective ratings may reflect the accumulated difficulty or loss of control experienced over the entire trial, whereas SCL may primarily reflect autonomic arousal elicited during the early phase of a salient control disruption.
Future studies are therefore needed to determine whether and under what conditions perturbation-induced autonomic arousal directly contributes to retrospective agency judgments.
The exploratory GAMM analyses further suggest that mean-level comparisons alone may obscure the temporal dynamics of perturbation-induced arousal.
Across the two experiments, SCL changes were characterized by time-varying trajectories rather than sustained elevations throughout the perturbation period.
Although these findings are exploratory, they highlight the potential value of modeling continuous physiological dynamics in studies of ongoing action control.
In the present study, we developed an experimental paradigm that allowed EDA to be tracked over an extended period of continuous control.

Unlike in typical SoA experiments where participants experienced perturbations across repeated trials lasting only a few seconds, participants in the present task rested for 2 minutes and performed a continuous control task for approximately 10 minutes.
This extended duration allowed us to track changes in SCL over a sufficiently long period before, during, and after the perturbation.
In addition, the perturbation angle was dynamically varied to avoid excessive repetition of identical perturbations.
Repeated exposure to similar events is known to attenuate EDA responses through habituation of the orienting response (Barry et al., 2023; Meir et al., 2024; Zimmer & Richter, 2023).

To date, both explicit and implicit measures of SoA have been developed, and their correlations have also been examined (Dewey & Knoblich, 2014; Imaizumi & Tanno, 2019; Siebertz & Jansen, 2022).

text.text: By contrast, implicit measures are intended to capture agency-related processes without requiring participants to directly report their experience.

A representative example is temporal binding (Barlas et al., 2018; Barlas & Obhi, 2014; Moore & Obhi, 2012; Muth et al., 2022), the perceived compression of the temporal interval between a voluntary action and its outcome.

text.text: Although temporal binding has often been used as an implicit index of SoA, accumulating evidence suggests that it does not necessarily correspond to subjective agency experience and may also reflect more general processes such as causal inference (Buehner, 2012; Dewey & Knoblich, 2014; Kirsch et al., 2019; Suzuki et al., 2019).

text.text: Given the limitations associated with both explicit and implicit measures of SoA, physiological measures may provide a complementary perspective on the processes accompanying changes in SoA, rather than an alternative measure of SoA itself.

The present findings suggest that EDA can capture the online temporal dynamics of autonomic arousal during disrupted control, including an early increase after perturbation onset and sustained elevation after perturbation offset-temporal characteristics that could not be captured by retrospective ratings.
Nevertheless, EDA should not be interpreted as a direct index of SoA on the basis of the present findings alone.

As an index of sympathetic arousal, EDA is sensitive to multiple emotional or cognitive processes, including stress (Chu et al., 2023; Setz et al., 2010), attention (Hartnett et al., 2025), and mental workload (Hogervorst et al., 2014).
text.formatted: As an index of sympathetic arousal, EDA is sensitive to multiple emotional or cognitive processes, including stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chu et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Setz et al., 2010)</ref>, attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hartnett et al., 2025)</ref>, and mental workload <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hogervorst et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, the observed increase in SCL indicates that disrupted control was accompanied by autonomic arousal, but does not establish a causal relationship between subjective SoA and autonomic arousal.
The perturbation may have independently reduced SoA and increased SCL.
Alternatively, consistent with the two-step account of SoA, perturbationinduced arousal may have served as an additional bodily cue contributing to retrospective agency inference.
Thus, combining physiological measures with established explicit and implicit measures may provide a more comprehensive characterization of the processes accompanying changes in SoA.
An important limitation is that perturbation magnitude also substantially affected task performance.
Participants completed markedly fewer successful reaches in the Strong than in the Weak condition, particularly during the perturbation period.
Therefore, the larger SCL response in the Strong condition cannot be attributed specifically to sensorimotor discrepancy or reduced SoA.
Greater task difficulty, effort, error frequency, uncertainty, or frustration associated with the stronger perturbation may also have contributed to the electrodermal response.
Future studies could dissociate these factors by manipulating control discrepancy while more closely matching task difficulty and performance across conditions.
Another limitation of the present study concerns the difference in the time periods captured by subjective and physiological measures.

The SoA and perceived stress ratings were obtained retrospectively at the end of each trial and therefore represented summary evaluations of the entire joystick-control period (10 minutes), including the baseline periods before and after the perturbation.
In contrast, the SCL analyses focused on predefined time windows relative to perturbation onset.
Although this approach was necessary to measure stable EDA, these ratings cannot be mapped one-to-one onto the magnitude or time course of physiological response at specific moments.

Accordingly, the apparent dissociation between subjective ratings and SCL across perturbation duration may partly reflect differences in measurement timescale rather than a fundamental dissociation between subjective and physiological responses.
In Experiment 2, the duration conditions also differed in the amount of unperturbed control between perturbation offset and the end-of-trial ratings.
Consequently, the observed rating differences cannot be attributed uniquely to perturbation duration.
In conclusion, the present study provides evidence that spatial perturbations during continuous action influence not only subjective SoA but also online autonomic arousal indexed by SCL.
The present findings suggest that the electrodermal response may remain elevated for some time after perturbation offset.
Together, these results indicate that the electrodermal response accompanying disrupted control has temporal characteristics that are not fully captured by retrospective subjective judgments.
By incorporating physiological measures into SoA research, the present study provides a complementary perspective on how disruptions of control unfold during ongoing action.
